title: Rs 1 Lakh Crore for Research, but PhD Scholars Wait Months for Their Stipends
excerpt: An India Today feature asks why young scientists are struggling while a Rs 1 lakh crore research corpus rolls out — as fellowship holders report months without pay and a poll finds a quarter of scholars netting under Rs 10,000 a month.
body:
• India's Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) corpus totals Rs 1 lakh crore (Rs 1 trillion) in long-term, low- or no-interest financing, and Rs 20,000 crore has been earmarked for an RDI scheme aimed mainly at private-sector research, according to Al Jazeera's analysis of government documents.
  • At the same time, the fellowship schemes that pay PhD scholars have shrunk: funding for the schemes folded into Vigyan Dhara fell 67.5% between 2016-17 and 2025-26, and INSPIRE fellows told Al Jazeera they had gone three to nine months without a stipend.
  • This month, National Fellowship for Scheduled Caste Students (NFSC) scholars wrote to MPs in a letter dated November 6, 2026, saying their September 2026 fellowship had not arrived, with the nodal agency blaming funds not released by the Social Justice Ministry.
  • An India Research Watch poll of 1,115 current and recent PhD scholars found 25% netting less than Rs 10,000 a month after fees, and 14% receiving no stipend at all.

India has announced a Rs 1 lakh crore corpus to finance research, development and innovation. Yet the young scientists that money is ultimately meant to serve are, in case after documented case, waiting months to be paid. An India Today feature this week poses the question directly: with a fund of that size, why are young scientists still struggling?

The reporting behind the question is not new, and it is specific. It concerns the fellowships — the monthly stipends that keep PhD scholars housed, fed and in their laboratories — and a pattern of delayed payments, shrinking scheme budgets and unanswered emails that scholars say is pushing some of them into debt and others out of research altogether.

Where the big money goes

The Rs 1 lakh crore RDI corpus, announced by the finance minister, is designed to provide long-term financing at low or no interest, according to Al Jazeera's analysis of government documents, budgets and interviews with researchers. Of that, Rs 20,000 crore was earmarked for a new RDI scheme targeting the private sector. In the current financial year, Al Jazeera found, 70 percent of the Department of Science and Technology's (DST) annual budget was allocated to a scheme providing interest-free loans to private companies conducting research in 'sunrise domains' such as semiconductors.

The stated aim, as Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and DST officials have explained it, is to make India a 'product nation', get more patents filed in India and curb the brain drain.

India's overall R&D expenditure reached 0.84% of GDP in 2023-24, still substantially below major technology economies, according to a Chronicle IAS analysis of India's R&D landscape. That analysis notes that the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF) and the Rs 1-lakh-crore RDI initiative 'offer opportunities, but their impact depends on transparent, timely funding and genuine risk-sharing', and that researchers confront delayed grants, rigid procurement rules and compliance burdens identified by NITI Aayog.

The stipend reality

For scholars, the system runs in the opposite direction. The INSPIRE scheme, funded by the DST, is meant to pay PhD fellows Rs 37,000 to Rs 42,000 a month for living expenses, plus Rs 20,000 a year for research costs. In 2024-25, 653 fellows were enrolled in its PhD fellowship. Al Jazeera spoke to nearly a dozen current and former INSPIRE fellows at IITs and IISERs; all had gone from three to as long as nine months without a stipend. 'For over a year now, many of us who are pursuing PhDs under DST-funded fellowships have not received our stipends,' INSPIRE fellow Sayali Atkare wrote on LinkedIn. 'This has pushed many young researchers into severe financial and emotional stress.'

The budgets behind the fellowships have also contracted. In January 2025 the government folded three R&D schemes into Vigyan Dhara and said funding had 'significantly increased' from Rs 3.30 billion to Rs 14.25 billion. The Rs 3.30 billion figure, Al Jazeera's budget analysis shows, covered only the scheme's launch quarter; the three predecessor schemes had a full-year budget of Rs 18.27 billion, making the new allocation a 22 percent decrease. Across the period since 2016-17, funding for Vigyan Dhara's constituent schemes fell 67.5%, from Rs 43.89 billion to Rs 14.25 billion.

DST Secretary Abhay Karandikar acknowledged the disbursement delays in May 2025 and told The Hindu he was 'aware' of the crisis, saying all problems had been addressed and scholars would be paid on time from June 2025. 'I don't foresee any issue in the future,' he said.

A live case, this month

The complaints have not stopped. Scheduled Caste research scholars under the NFSC scheme had not received their fellowship for September 2026, Maktoob Media reported, and the National Fellowship Cell at the NSFDC told them the delay was because the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment had not released the funds. In a letter to MPs dated November 6, 2026, the scholars sought 'urgent intervention'. 'The NFSC fellowship is not merely a stipend; it is a constitutional and social commitment to enable Scheduled Caste students to pursue advanced research with dignity and without financial insecurity,' the letter says.

The scheme's guidelines say fellows should be paid by the 15th of every month once universities issue continuation certificates. The scholars' letter documents how far practice sits from that rule: the Rs 37,000 instalments for October and November 2024 were both credited only on December 6, 2024, and the December instalment arrived on March 3, 2025. The scholars have asked for funds to be released in advance, a public monthly dashboard tracking releases, and a time-bound grievance system.

How widespread the squeeze is

Beyond the named schemes, an India Research Watch (IRW) LinkedIn poll of 1,115 current and recent PhD scholars — measuring stipends net of fees — found 11% earning less than Rs 10,000 a month and a further 14% receiving zero or negative stipends, effectively researching without financial support, while 40% received more than Rs 30,000. IRW founder Achal Agrawal estimated that raising every scholar below Rs 10,000 by Rs 10,000 a month — assuming 50,000 students — would cost about Rs 600 crore a year, and contrasted that with the nearly Rs 2,000 crore public institutions spend annually on journal subscriptions under the One Nation One Subscription scheme. Low or no stipends, the poll report notes, push scholars into part-time work, prolong research timelines, or force them to abandon PhD programmes.

'The government throws around big terms, but those toiling in laboratories are suffering.'

— Lal Chandra Vishwakarma, president, All-India Research Scholars Association, to Al Jazeera

What to watch

The gap the India Today feature identifies is, on the documented evidence, a gap between two different kinds of money: large, loan-based funds aimed at companies, and the small monthly transfers that university research actually runs on. Whether the RDI corpus and the ANRF change the second picture depends on the unglamorous machinery scholars keep naming — release dates, dashboards, grievance timelines. The NFSC scholars' asks are now with MPs. For diaspora researchers weighing a return to Indian academia, and for families abroad supporting a PhD student in India, that machinery — not the headline corpus — is what determines whether a research career in India pays its own rent.
image_caption: An editorial illustration shows a vault of research funds feeding a pipe wrapped in red tape, with scholars collecting a trickle of coins below. India has a Rs 1 lakh crore research and innovation corpus, while many PhD fellows report stipend delays of months.
nri_angle: For Indian researchers abroad weighing a return, and for diaspora families funding PhD students in India, the gap between headline research money and on-time stipends shapes whether talent stays, leaves, or comes back.
author: Diaspora Desk
